title: Maryland gets ‘thumbs down’ after reducing funding for tobacco control programs
summary: An annual report evaluating statewide tobacco regulations marked Maryland down for cutting $5 million from tobacco prevention programs, at a time when uncertain federal funding and support make state-level actions more influential than ever.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 28, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 28, 2026

An annual report evaluating statewide tobacco regulations marked Maryland down for cutting $5 million from tobacco prevention programs, at a time when federal funding and support is not guaranteed and advocates say state-level actions are more influential than ever.

The American Lung Association released its annual State of Tobacco Control Report Wednesday, which grades states on various policy categories to help reduce tobacco use.

For Maryland, much of the report card was unchanged from the previous year, with high marks in some areas and low marks in others. But with a $5 million drop in state funds for tobacco control and prevention, the association gave Maryland a “thumbs down” as part of the state’s overall report card.

Dr. Panagis Galiatsatos, a spokesperson for the American Lung Association National and an assistant professor for Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, said that now is not the time to “take our foot off the gas” for prevention funding and programs.

“Addiction to nicotine can become lifelong,” Galiatsatos said. “This isn’t an addiction that gets you high or inebriated or intoxicated, so the intention behind it is to introduce it to every facet of your life, so when you go through the motions of your daily habits, you’re constantly triggered to use these products.”

According to the report, Maryland’s funding for tobacco control programs dropped compared to last year’s. For fiscal year 2026, Maryland provided $16.3 million in state funding for tobacco prevention and control programs. That’s down from $21.3 million allocated from the year before.

And with the state facing another $1.6 billion budget deficit in the current session, more cuts may be on the line.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention best practices suggest that Maryland should be spending closer to $48 million on prevention programs. The lung association gave Maryland an “F” for its prevention-funding – along with 38 other states and Washington, D.C. The organization urges Maryland and many others to boost funding for prevention efforts.

But Aleks Casper, the association’s advocacy director for Maryland, Delaware, Virginia and Washington, D.C., notes that funding is just part of a system of policies that help reduce tobacco use and said Maryland has led the way on other policy areas.

“You have to look at the whole picture. None of it can be done in silos,” Casper said. “The reason we grade in these multiple categories is that they all work together. They’re all pieces of the puzzle that fit together … If we can prevent people from ever starting to use the products and support them when they’re ready to quit, those are our big puzzle pieces.”

In last year’s report, the American Lung Association held up Maryland as the “most improved” state due to an expansion of the Clean Indoor Air Act to include e-cigarettes as well an increase to the cigarette tax from $3.75 to $5.00.

The tobacco tax earns the statea “B” in the tobacco taxes category and the Clean Indoor Air Act earns it an “A” in the smoke-free air category, both unchanged from the year before

But Casper said that the drop in funding also affected the state’s score for the category rating access to cessation services. Last year, Maryland had an “A” in that category for its Medicaid coverage for helpful medications and access to some counseling for people trying to quit tobacco products. But the drop in funding also dropped Maryland’s score to a “B” in the 2026 report, Casper said.

Lawmakers have not passed legislation that would limit or ban flavored tobacco products in the state, a key policy stance to help reduce the number of youths who take up smoking or vaping. Maryland continues to earn an “F” in that category, along with 46 other states.

New tobacco tax, regulations boost Maryland’s standing with American Lung Association

“In comparison to other states, I think we can be proud of what the report shows. At the same time … we clearly have a lot more to do,” Galiatsatos said. “It’s important not to look at this report as static — like we’ve done our job. We have to be dynamic. Because there’s many things that the tobacco industry is, but one of them is not a quitter.

“They’re going to continue pushing for their products in various ways,” he said. “That’s where I think the report really captured Maryland’s attempts toward public health matters around tobacco.”

Smaller decisions can also decrease tobacco use, Galiatsatos noted. In 2024, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott (D) approved legislation that banned tobacco use in Camden Yards and at M&T Bank Stadium.

The ordinance is aimed at “ending the longstanding link between baseball and smokeless tobacco and preventing youth use of harmful and addictive tobacco products, especially by student athletes who imitate their role models on and off the field,” Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids said in a statement at that time.

“I think that should get highlighted,” Galiatsatos said, “Like I said, we should be proud of the work we’ve done but mindful that there’s a lot more work to do.”

But the American Lung Association says that policy decisions at the state-level are more crucial than ever, as the Trump administration could continue to disrupt funding and operations for federal programs that help states with tobacco-use reduction efforts.

“When you look at tobacco prevention and control policies from a national perspective and a federal perspective, 2025 was really a devastating year for us,” said Casper said.

The 2026 report says that staffing reductions at the CDC and the Food and Drug Administration caused “significant disruption to operations.”

“This unprecedented loss of federal capacity marked one of the most significant setbacks in tobacco prevention and control in decades,” the report says. “It creates an opening for the tobacco industry to expand its reach and target new users, which will have consequences on tobacco use rates in the U.S.”

Last year, the administration also delayed grant payment to support efforts in tobacco control, which caused “extensive damage” to those programs. Policy actions that fast-track FDA-approval of specific nicotine and tobacco products also concern the American Lung Association.

“With all of this uncertainty at the federal level,” Casper said, “It is now more important than ever that states really look to see what they can do to ensure that these continue and that there are robust programs available.”
